Total number of living humans on Earth

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/World_Population_Prospects.svg/500px-World_Population_Prospects.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:World_Population_Prospects.svg)

High, medium, and low projections of the future human world population[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:4-1)

In [world demographics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_the_world "Demographics of the world"), the **world population** is the total number of humans currently alive. It was estimated by the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") to have [exceeded 8 billion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_Eight_Billion "Day of Eight Billion") (8,000,000,000) on November 15, 2022. It took around 300,000 years of human [prehistory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistory "Prehistory") and [history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_history "Human history") for the human population to reach a billion and only 218 more years from there to reach 8 billion. As of 2026, the world population is approximately 8.3 billion.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:5-2) However, this figure is only a very rough approximation (see §History).

The human population experienced [continuous growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_growth "Population growth") following the [Great Famine of 1315–1317](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Famine_of_1315%E2%80%931317 "Great Famine of 1315–1317") and the end of the [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death") in 1350, when it had reached nearly 370 million.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-3) The highest global [population growth rates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_population_growth_rate "List of countries by population growth rate"), with increases of over 1.8% per year, occurred between 1955 and 1975, peaking at 2.1% between 1965 and 1970.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:1-4) The growth rate declined to 1.1% between 2015 and 2020 and is projected to decline further in the 21st century.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:8-5) The global population is still increasing, but there is significant uncertainty about its long-term trajectory due to changing [fertility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_fertility_rate "Total fertility rate") and [mortality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortality_rate "Mortality rate") rates.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-6) The [UN Department of Economics and Social Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_Department_of_Economics_and_Social_Affairs "UN Department of Economics and Social Affairs") (UNDESA) has projected the world population to reach between 9 and 10 billion people by 2050, providing an 80% [confidence interval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_interval "Confidence interval") of 10–12 billion by the end of the 21st century,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:4-1) with a growth rate by then of zero. However, other [demographers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demography "Demography") predict that the human population may begin to decline in the second half of the 21st century if global fertility rates continue to fall.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-7)

The total number of births globally, as of 2024, is approximately 132 million/year, which is projected to peak during the period 2040–2045 at 141 million/year and then decline slowly to 126 million/year by 2100.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:9-8) The total number of deaths is currently 63 million/year and is projected to grow steadily to 122 million/year by 2100.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:9-8)

The [global median age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_pyramid "Population pyramid") of human beings, as of 2026, is 31.1 years.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:0-9)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:5-2)

## History

Further information: [Estimates of historical world population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estimates_of_historical_world_population "Estimates of historical world population") and [Human history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_history "Human history")

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Illustration_of_contemporary_and_past_human_populations_Our_World_in_Data.png/330px-Illustration_of_contemporary_and_past_human_populations_Our_World_in_Data.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Illustration_of_contemporary_and_past_human_populations_Our_World_in_Data.png)

Visual comparison of the world population in past and present

Estimates of world population by their nature are an aspect of [modernity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernity "Modernity"), possible only since the [Age of Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Discovery "Age of Discovery"). Early estimates for the population of the world[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-10) date to the 17th century: [William Petty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Petty "William Petty"), in 1682, estimated the world population at 320 million (current estimates ranging close to twice this number); by the late 18th century, estimates ranged close to one billion (consistent with current estimates).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-11) More refined estimates, broken down by continents, were published in the first half of the 19th century, at 600 million to 1 billion in the early 1800s and 800 million to 1 billion in the 1840s.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-12)

It is difficult for estimates to be better than rough approximations, as even current population estimates are fraught with uncertainties from 3% to 5%.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-Kapitza2-13)

### Prehistoric patterns

The history of the world's population involves a great deal of speculation. Before 9000 BC, virtually all humans were hunter-gatherers living in small bands that usually verged on the edge of extinction. Survival depended on the capture of hunted animals; if supply of animals dwindled for any reason, humans would starve; if the human population grew too large the number of surviving animals would shrink,leading to starvation the next year for the hunters (humans had not yet invented the technique of domesticating and herding animals). The hunting cultures sometimes fished, and usually gathered wild seeds and nuts, but they did not plant or grow vegetables or any other crops. One very rough estimate is 8 million hunters lived circa 9000 BC when the first of several "[agricultural revolutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic_Revolution "Neolithic Revolution")"occurred in the eastern hemisphere (the dates are very conjectural). Around the year 9000 BC in the Middle East,for reasons unknown, some groups began to domesticate and graze sheep. The practice of cultivating plants was invented independently in three places: in the Middle East and Europe (wheat, 6500–3500 BC), in Southeast Asia (rice,6800–4000 BC), and in Central America and Peru (corn, about 2500 BC).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-14)

Agriculture provided a steady food supply that could be stored for a year or longer in order to minimize the risk of famine. Farm production could be expanded by systematic human exertion. The new technology of farming meant that the food supply was proportional to the number of workers who could plant and harvest the crops. Every new pair of hands meant more food for the community, so children were valued in agricultural societies. Later, additional workers found useful work in building irrigation canals and systems that provided a stable water supply for crops, especially in Egypt, Mesopotamia, India, China, Peru and Mexico. The population could now grow because new people paid their own way. (It would take many centuries before the arable land supply became a limiting factor.) However, death rates were high, especially for infants and children, so even with high birth rates growth was slow. The same amount of land could support either 1,000 hunters or 100,000 farmers, and thus farmers ultimately won the fight for the land. Farmers gathered in permanent villages, and through a process of warfare consolidated into much larger states, including those in China, India, Egypt and Mesopotamia. From 300 to 1400 AD large agricultural states also existed throughout the eastern United States, called the "[Hopewell tradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopewell_tradition "Hopewell tradition")" and "[Mississippian cultures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippian_cultures "Mississippian cultures")". They are most famous as [Mound Builders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound_Builders "Mound Builders"), but their culture collapsed (for unknown reasons) by 1500. The natives encountered by the English and French were nomadic hunters who supplemented their meat diet with cultivated vegetables.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-16)

### Ancient and post-classical history

Main articles: [Classical demography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_demography "Classical demography") and [Medieval demography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_demography "Medieval demography")

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Population_curve.svg/500px-Population_curve.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Population_curve.svg)

Graph of human population from 10 000 BC to 2000 [AD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anno_Domini "Anno Domini"). It shows exponential rise in world population that has taken place since the end of the seventeenth century.

Estimates of the population of the world at the time agriculture emerged in around 10,000 BC have ranged between 1 million and 15 million.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-18) Even earlier, genetic evidence suggests humans may have gone through a population bottleneck of between 1,000 and 10,000 people about 70,000 BC, according to the now largely discredited [Toba catastrophe theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toba_catastrophe_theory "Toba catastrophe theory"). By contrast, it is estimated that around 50–60 million people lived in the combined eastern and western [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") in the 4th century AD.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-19)

The [Plague of Justinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plague_of_Justinian "Plague of Justinian") caused Europe's population to drop by around 50% between the 6th and 8th centuries AD.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-20) The population of Europe was more than 70 million in 1340.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-21) From 1340 to 1400, the world's population fell from an estimated 443 million to 350–375 million,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-22) with the [Indian subcontinent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_subcontinent "Indian subcontinent") suffering the most tremendous loss and Europe suffering the [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death")[pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandemic "Pandemic");[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-Essai_sur_l'%C3%A9volution_du_nombre_des_hommes-23) it took 200 years for European population figures to recover.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-24) The population of China decreased from 123 million in 1200 to 65 million in 1393,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-25) presumably from a combination of [Mongol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_Empire "Mongol Empire") invasions, famine, and plague.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-26)

Starting in AD 2, the [Han dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty "Han dynasty") of [ancient China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_China "Ancient China") kept consistent family registers to properly assess the poll taxes and labor service duties of each household.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-nishijima_1986_pp595-96-27) In that year, the population of [Western Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Han "Western Han") was recorded as 57,671,400 individuals in 12,366,470 households, decreasing to 47,566,772 individuals in 9,348,227 households by AD 146, towards the [end of the Han dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_the_Han_dynasty "End of the Han dynasty").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-nishijima_1986_pp595-96-27) From 200 to 400, the world population fell from an estimated 257 million to 206 million, with China suffering the greatest loss.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-Essai_sur_l'%C3%A9volution_du_nombre_des_hommes-23) At the founding of the [Ming dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_dynasty "Ming dynasty") in 1368, China's population was reported to be close to 60 million; toward the end of the dynasty in 1644, it may have approached 150 million.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-28) England's population reached an estimated 5.6 million in 1650, up from an estimated 2.6 million in 1500.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-29) New crops that were brought to Asia and Europe from the Americas by Portuguese and Spanish colonists in the 16th century are believed to have contributed to population growth.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-32) Since their introduction to Africa by Portuguese traders in the 16th century,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-33) maize and [cassava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassava "Cassava") have similarly replaced traditional African crops as the most important [staple food](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staple_food "Staple food") crops grown on the continent.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-34)

The [pre-Columbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Columbian_era "Pre-Columbian era") population of the Americas is uncertain; historian David Henige called it "the most unanswerable question in the world."[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-35) By the end of the 20th century, scholarly consensus favored an estimate of roughly 55 million people, but numbers from various sources have ranged from 10 million to 100 million.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-36) Encounters between European explorers and populations in the rest of the world often introduced local [epidemics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_epidemics "List of epidemics") of extraordinary virulence.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-37) According to the most extreme scholarly claims, as many as 90% of the [Native American population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_history_of_the_Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Population history of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas") of the [New World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World "New World") died of [Old World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_World "Old World") diseases such as [smallpox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox "Smallpox"), [measles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measles "Measles"), and [influenza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Influenza "Influenza").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-38) Over the centuries, the Europeans had developed high degrees of immunity to these diseases, while the indigenous peoples had no such immunity.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-39)

### Modern history

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Cities_with_1M_People_in_2025.png/500px-Cities_with_1M_People_in_2025.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cities_with_1M_People_in_2025.png)

Map showing urban areas with at least one million inhabitants in 2025. Only 3% of the world's population lived in urban areas in 1800; this proportion had risen to 47% by 2000, and reached 56% by 2020.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-40)

During the European [Agricultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Agricultural_Revolution "British Agricultural Revolution") and [Industrial Revolutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution"), the [life expectancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_expectancy "Life expectancy") of children increased dramatically.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-41) The percentage of the children born in London who [died before the age of five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infant_mortality "Infant mortality") decreased from 74.5% in 1730–1749 to 31.8% in 1810–1829.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-Buer-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-43) Between 1700 and 1900, Europe's population increased from about 100 million to over 400 million.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-44) Altogether, the areas populated by people of European descent comprised 36% of the world's population in 1900.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-45)

Population growth in the Western world became more rapid after the introduction of [vaccination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaccination "Vaccination") and other improvements in medicine and [sanitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanitation "Sanitation").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-46) Improved material conditions led to the population of Britain increasing from 10 million to 40 million in the 19th century.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-47) The population of the United Kingdom reached 60 million in 2006.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-48) The United States saw its population grow from around 5.3 million in 1800 to 106 million in 1920, exceeding 307 million in 2010.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-49)

### 20th century

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Global_population_after_1820.png/500px-Global_population_after_1820.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Global_population_after_1820.png)

The human population grew by approximately 4.5 billion people during the 20th century, increasing from about 1.6 billion in 1900 to just over 6 billion by the year 2000.

The first half of the 20th century in [Imperial Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire") and the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") was marked by a succession of major wars, [famines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famine "Famine") and other disasters which caused large-scale population losses (approximately 60 million excess deaths).[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-51) After the collapse of the Soviet Union, Russia's population declined significantly – from 150 million in 1991 to 143 million in 2012[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-52) – but by 2013 this decline appeared to have halted.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-53)

Many countries in the [developing world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developing_world "Developing world") have experienced extremely rapid population growth since the early 20th century, due to economic development and improvements in public health. China's population rose from approximately 430 million in 1850 to 580 million in 1953,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-54) and now stands at over 1.3 billion. The population of the [Indian subcontinent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_subcontinent "Indian subcontinent"), which was about 125 million in 1750, increased to 389 million in 1941;[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-55) today, India, Pakistan and Bangladesh are collectively home to about 1.63 billion people.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-56)[Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java "Java"), an island in [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia"), had about 5 million inhabitants in 1815; it had a population of over 139 million in 2020.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-57) In just one hundred years, the population of Brazil decupled (x10), from about 17 million in 1900, or about 1% of the world population in that year, to about 176 million in 2000, or almost 3% of the global population in the very early 21st century. Mexico's population grew from 13.6 million in 1900 to about 112 million in 2010.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-59) Between the 1920s and 2000s, Kenya's population grew from 2.9 million to 37 million.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-60)

The UN estimated that the world population reached one billion for the first time in 1804. It was another 123 years before it reached two billion in 1927, but it took only 33 years to reach three billion in 1960.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-un2004-62) Thereafter, it took 14 years for the global population to reach four billion in 1974, 13 years to reach five billion in 1987, 12 years to reach six billion in 1999 and, according to the United States Census Bureau, 13 years to reach seven billion in March 2012.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-USCBcite-63) The United Nations, however, estimated that the world population reached seven billion in October 2011.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-UN7bn-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-Guardian7-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-UPI7bn-66)

According to the UN, the global population reached eight billion in November 2022,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-auto-67) but because the growth rate is slowing, it will take another 15 years to reach around 9 billion by 2037 and 20 years to reach 10 billion by 2057.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:7-68) Alternative scenarios for 2050 range from a low of 7.4 billion to a high of more than 10.6 billion.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-WorldPopProspects-69) Projected figures vary depending on underlying statistical assumptions and the variables used in projection calculations, especially the [fertility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fertility "Fertility") and [mortality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortality_rate "Mortality rate") variables. Long-range predictions to 2150 range from a population decline to 3.2 billion in the "low scenario", to "high scenarios" of 24.8 billion.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-WorldPopProspects-69) One extreme scenario predicted a massive increase to 256 billion by 2150, assuming the global fertility rate remained at its 1995 level of 3.04 children per woman; however, by 2010 the global fertility rate had declined to 2.52.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-LongRangeProjections2003KeyFindings-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-Fertility2010-71)

There is no estimation for the exact day or month the world's population surpassed one or two billion. The points at which it reached three and four billion were not officially noted, but the International Database of the United States Census Bureau placed them in July 1959 and April 1974 respectively. The United Nations did determine, and commemorate, the "Day of 5 Billion" on 11 July 1987, and the "Day of 6 Billion" on 12 October 1999. The Population Division of the United Nations declared the "[Day of Seven Billion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_Seven_Billion "Day of Seven Billion")" to be 31 October 2011.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-72) The United Nations marked the birth of the [eight billionth person](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinice_Mabansag "Vinice Mabansag") on 15 November 2022.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-73)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-auto-67)

 2015 map showing average life expectancy by country in years. In 2015, the World Health Organization estimated the average global life expectancy as 71.4 years.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-WHOStats2016-74)

As of 2020, the global [sex ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_sex_ratio "Human sex ratio") is approximately 1.01 males to 1 female.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-cia-factbook-75) Approximately 24.7% of the global population is aged under 15, while 65.2% is aged 15–64 and 10.1% is aged 65 or over.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-cia-factbook-75) The median age of the world's population is estimated to be 31 years in 2020,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:0-9) and is expected to rise to 37.9 years by 2050.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-76)

According to the [World Health Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Health_Organization "World Health Organization"), the global average [life expectancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_life_expectancy "List of countries by life expectancy") is 73.3 years as of 2020, with women living an average of 75.9 years and men approximately 70.8 years.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-77) In 2010, the global [fertility rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fertility_rate "Fertility rate") was estimated at 2.44 children per woman.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-78) In June 2012, British researchers calculated the total weight of Earth's human population as approximately 287 million tonnes (630 billion pounds), with the average person weighing around 62 kilograms (137 lb).[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-79)

The [IMF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund "International Monetary Fund") estimated nominal 2021 [gross world product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_world_product "Gross world product") at US$94.94 trillion, giving an annual global per capita figure of around US$12,290.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-80) Around 9.3% of the world population lives in [extreme poverty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_poverty "Extreme poverty"), subsisting on less than US$1.9 per day;[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-81) around 8.9% are [malnourished](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malnutrition "Malnutrition").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-82) 87% of the world's over-15s are considered [literate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literacy_rate "Literacy rate").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-83) As of January 2024, there were about 5 billion global Internet users, constituting 66% of the world population.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-84)

The [Han Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Chinese "Han Chinese") are the world's largest single ethnic group, constituting over 19% of the global population in 2011.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-85) The world's most-spoken languages[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-86) are [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language") (1.132B), [Mandarin Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandarin_Chinese "Mandarin Chinese") (1.117B), [Hindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi "Hindi") (615M), [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language") (534M) and [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language") (280M). More than three billion people speak an Indo-European language, which is the largest language family by number of speakers. Standard Arabic is a language with no native speakers, but the total number of speakers is estimated at 274 million people.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-87)

The largest religious categories in the world as of 2020 are estimated as follows: [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") (31%), [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") (25%), [Unaffiliated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irreligion "Irreligion") (16%) and [Hinduism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinduism "Hinduism") (15%).[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-Pew-88)

Population by continent (2022 data)

Six of the Earth's seven [continents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continent "Continent") are permanently inhabited on a large scale. Asia is the most populous continent, with its 4.64 billion inhabitants accounting for 60% of the world population. The world's two most populated countries, India and China, together constitute about 36% of the world's population. Africa is the second most populated continent, with around 1.34 billion people, or 17% of the world's population. Europe's 747 million people make up 10% of the world's population as of 2020, while the [Latin American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_American "Latin American") and [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean") regions are home to around 653 million (8%). Northern America, primarily consisting of the United States and Canada, has a population of around 368 million (5%), and Oceania, the least populated region, has about 42 million inhabitants (0.5%).[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-89)[Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica "Antarctica") only has a very small, fluctuating population of about 1200 people based mainly in polar [science stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_stations_in_Antarctica "Research stations in Antarctica").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-AntarcticCIA-90)

## Fluctuation

Main articles: [Population growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_growth "Population growth"), [Human population projections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_population_projections "Human population projections"), and [Population dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_dynamics "Population dynamics")

[![Image 75](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/World_population_%28UN%29.svg/500px-World_population_%28UN%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:World_population_(UN).svg)

Estimates of population evolution in different [continents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continent "Continent") between 1950 and 2050, according to the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations"). The vertical axis is [logarithmic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logarithmic_scale "Logarithmic scale") and is in millions of people.

Population size fluctuates at differing rates in differing regions. Nonetheless, population growth has been the long-standing trend on all inhabited continents, as well as in most individual states. During the 20th century, the global population saw its greatest increase in known history, rising from about 1.6 billion in 1900 to over 6 billion in 2000[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-111) as the whole world entered the early phases of what has come to be called the "[demographic transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographic_transition "Demographic transition")". Some of the key factors contributing to this increase included the lessening of the [mortality rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortality_rate "Mortality rate") in many countries by improved sanitation and [medical advances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_medicine#Modern_medicine "History of medicine"), and a massive increase in agricultural productivity attributed to the [Green Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Revolution "Green Revolution").[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-112)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-113) By 2000, there were approximately ten times as many people on Earth as there had been in 1700.

However, this rapid growth did not last. During the period 2000–2005, the United Nations estimates that the world's population was growing at an annual rate of 1.3% (equivalent to around 80 million people), down from a peak of 2.1% during the period 1965–1970.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:8-5) Globally, although the population [growth rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_growth "Population growth") has been steadily declining from its peak in 1968,[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-114) growth [still remains high](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projections_of_population_growth#Growth_regions "Projections of population growth") in [Sub-Saharan Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-Saharan_Africa "Sub-Saharan Africa").[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-115)

[![Image 76](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/Total_Fertility_Rate_Map_by_Country.svg/500px-Total_Fertility_Rate_Map_by_Country.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Total_Fertility_Rate_Map_by_Country.svg)

Map of countries by [total fertility rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_sovereign_states_and_dependencies_by_total_fertility_rate "List of sovereign states and dependencies by total fertility rate") (2022–2023), referring to the average number of children that are born to a woman over her lifetime, according to the [Population Reference Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_Reference_Bureau "Population Reference Bureau")[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-116)

[![Image 77](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/World_population_counter%2C_Eureka%2C_Halifax%2C_West_Yorkshire_%2827th_August_2022%29_001.jpg/500px-World_population_counter%2C_Eureka%2C_Halifax%2C_West_Yorkshire_%2827th_August_2022%29_001.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:World_population_counter,_Eureka,_Halifax,_West_Yorkshire_(27th_August_2022)_001.jpg)

A world population clock in August 2022 at the [Eureka! Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eureka!_(museum) "Eureka! (museum)") in [Halifax, West Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax,_West_Yorkshire "Halifax, West Yorkshire"), England

In fact, during the 2010s, Japan and some countries in Europe began to [reduce in population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_decline "Population decline"), due to [sub-replacement fertility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-replacement_fertility "Sub-replacement fertility") rates.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-BigDecline-110)

In 2019, the United Nations reported that the rate of population growth continues to decline due to the ongoing global demographic transition. If this trend continues, the rate of growth may diminish to zero by 2100, concurrent with a world population plateau of 10.9 billion.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:8-5)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:7-68) However, this is only one of many estimates published by the UN; in 2009, UN population projections for 2050 ranged between around 8 billion and 10.5 billion.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-117) An alternative scenario is given by the statistician Jorgen Randers, who argues that traditional projections insufficiently take into account the downward impact of global urbanization on fertility. Randers' "most likely scenario" reveals a peak in the world population in the early 2040s at about 8.1 billion people, followed by decline.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-118) Adrian Raftery, a [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") professor of statistics and of sociology, states that "there's a 70 percent probability the world population will not stabilize this century. Population, which had sort of fallen off the world's agenda, remains a very important issue."[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-119)

World population by age group projection until 2100[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-q917-130)

Long-term global population growth is difficult to predict. The United Nations and the US Census Bureau both give different estimates – according to the UN, the world population reached seven billion in late 2011,[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-UN-121) while the USCB asserted that this occurred in March 2012.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-131) Since 1951, the UN has issued multiple projections of future world population, based on different assumptions. From 2000 to 2005, the UN consistently revised these projections downward, until the 2006 revision, issued on 14 March 2007, revised the 2050 mid-range estimate upwards by 273 million.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Complicating the UN's and others' attempts to project future populations is the fact that average global [birth rates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_rate "Birth rate"), as well as [mortality rates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortality_rate "Mortality rate"), are declining rapidly, as the nations of the world progress through the stages of the demographic transition, but both vary greatly between developed countries (where birth rates and mortality rates are often low) and developing countries (where birth and mortality rates typically remain high). Different ethnicities also display varying birth rates.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-132) Birth rate and mortality rates can change rapidly due to [disease epidemics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infectious_disease#Mortality_from_infectious_diseases "Infectious disease"), [wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_wars "List of wars") and other mass catastrophes, or [advances in medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_extension "Life extension") and [public health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_health "Public health").

Regional and worldwide populations after 1950. Projected population to 2100 is based on the UN's medium population scenario.

The UN's first report in 1951 showed that during the period 1950–55 the [crude birth rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_rate "Birth rate") was 36.9/1,000 population and the [crude death rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortality_rate "Mortality rate") was 19.1/1,000. By the period 2015–20, both numbers had dropped significantly to 18.5/1,000 for the crude birth rate and 7.5/1,000 for the crude death rate. UN projections for 2100 show a further decline in the crude birth rate to 11.6/1,000 and an increase in the crude death rate to 11.2/1,000.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:3-133)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:7-68)

The total number of births globally is currently (2015–20) 140 million/year, is projected to peak during the period 2040–45 at 141 million/year and thereafter decline slowly to 126 million/year by 2100.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:2-134) The total number of deaths is currently 57 million/year and is projected to grow steadily to 121 million/year by 2100.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:3-133)

2012 United Nations projections show a continued increase in population in the near future with a steady decline in population growth rate; the global population is expected to reach between 8.3 and 10.9 billion by 2050.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-135)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-136) 2003 [UN Population Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Population_Division "United Nations Population Division") population projections for the year 2150 range between 3.2 and 24.8 billion.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-LongRangeProjections2003KeyFindings-70) One of many independent mathematical models supports the lower estimate,[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-137) while a 2014 estimate forecasts between 9.3 and 12.6 billion in 2100, and continued growth thereafter.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-138)[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-139) The 2019 Revision of the UN estimates gives the "medium variant" population as; nearly 8.6 billion in 2030, about 9.7 billion in 2050 and about 10.9 billion in 2100.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-140) In December 2019, the [German Foundation for World Population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Foundation_for_World_Population "German Foundation for World Population") projected that the global population will reach 8 billion by 2023 as it increases by 156 every minute.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-141) In a modeled future projection by the [Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_for_Health_Metrics_and_Evaluation "Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation"), the global population was projected to peak in 2064 at 9.73 billion people and decline to 8.79 billion in 2100.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-142) Some analysts have questioned the sustainability of further world population growth, highlighting the [growing pressures on the environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_impact_on_the_environment "Human impact on the environment"),[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-StokstadAAAS-143)[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-144) global food supplies, and energy resources.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-145)[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-TIMEenvir-146)[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-Zehner-147)

Some scholars have argued that a form of "cultural selection" may be occurring due to significant differences in fertility rates between cultures, and it can therefore be expected that fertility rates and rates of population growth may rise again in the future.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-148)[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-149)[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-150) An example is certain religious groups that have a higher birth rate that is not accounted for by differences in income. In his book _Shall the Religious Inherit the Earth?_, [Eric Kaufmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Kaufmann "Eric Kaufmann") argues that demographic trends point to religious fundamentalists greatly increasing as a share of the population over the next century.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-151)[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-152) From the perspective of [evolutionary psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolutionary_psychology "Evolutionary psychology"), it is expected that selection pressure should occur for whatever psychological or cultural traits maximize fertility.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-153)[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-154)[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-bbc_sure-155)

Total number of living humans on Earth

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/World_Population_Prospects.svg/500px-World_Population_Prospects.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:World_Population_Prospects.svg)

High, medium, and low projections of the future human world population[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:4-1)

In [world demographics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_the_world "Demographics of the world"), the **world population** is the total number of humans currently alive. It was estimated by the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") to have [exceeded 8 billion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_Eight_Billion "Day of Eight Billion") (8,000,000,000) on November 15, 2022. It took around 300,000 years of human [prehistory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistory "Prehistory") and [history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_history "Human history") for the human population to reach a billion and only 218 more years from there to reach 8 billion. As of 2026, the world population is approximately 8.3 billion.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:5-2) However, this figure is only a very rough approximation (see §History).

The human population experienced [continuous growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_growth "Population growth") following the [Great Famine of 1315–1317](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Famine_of_1315%E2%80%931317 "Great Famine of 1315–1317") and the end of the [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death") in 1350, when it had reached nearly 370 million.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-3) The highest global [population growth rates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_population_growth_rate "List of countries by population growth rate"), with increases of over 1.8% per year, occurred between 1955 and 1975, peaking at 2.1% between 1965 and 1970.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:1-4) The growth rate declined to 1.1% between 2015 and 2020 and is projected to decline further in the 21st century.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:8-5) The global population is still increasing, but there is significant uncertainty about its long-term trajectory due to changing [fertility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_fertility_rate "Total fertility rate") and [mortality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortality_rate "Mortality rate") rates.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-6) The [UN Department of Economics and Social Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_Department_of_Economics_and_Social_Affairs "UN Department of Economics and Social Affairs") (UNDESA) has projected the world population to reach between 9 and 10 billion people by 2050, providing an 80% [confidence interval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_interval "Confidence interval") of 10–12 billion by the end of the 21st century,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:4-1) with a growth rate by then of zero. However, other [demographers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demography "Demography") predict that the human population may begin to decline in the second half of the 21st century if global fertility rates continue to fall.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-7)

The total number of births globally, as of 2024, is approximately 132 million/year, which is projected to peak during the period 2040–2045 at 141 million/year and then decline slowly to 126 million/year by 2100.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:9-8) The total number of deaths is currently 63 million/year and is projected to grow steadily to 122 million/year by 2100.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:9-8)

The [global median age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_pyramid "Population pyramid") of human beings, as of 2026, is 31.1 years.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:0-9)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:5-2)

## History

Further information: [Estimates of historical world population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estimates_of_historical_world_population "Estimates of historical world population") and [Human history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_history "Human history")

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Illustration_of_contemporary_and_past_human_populations_Our_World_in_Data.png/330px-Illustration_of_contemporary_and_past_human_populations_Our_World_in_Data.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Illustration_of_contemporary_and_past_human_populations_Our_World_in_Data.png)

Visual comparison of the world population in past and present

Estimates of world population by their nature are an aspect of [modernity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernity "Modernity"), possible only since the [Age of Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Discovery "Age of Discovery"). Early estimates for the population of the world[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-10) date to the 17th century: [William Petty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Petty "William Petty"), in 1682, estimated the world population at 320 million (current estimates ranging close to twice this number); by the late 18th century, estimates ranged close to one billion (consistent with current estimates).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-11) More refined estimates, broken down by continents, were published in the first half of the 19th century, at 600 million to 1 billion in the early 1800s and 800 million to 1 billion in the 1840s.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-12)

It is difficult for estimates to be better than rough approximations, as even current population estimates are fraught with uncertainties from 3% to 5%.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-Kapitza2-13)

### Prehistoric patterns

The history of the world's population involves a great deal of speculation. Before 9000 BC, virtually all humans were hunter-gatherers living in small bands that usually verged on the edge of extinction. Survival depended on the capture of hunted animals; if supply of animals dwindled for any reason, humans would starve; if the human population grew too large the number of surviving animals would shrink,leading to starvation the next year for the hunters (humans had not yet invented the technique of domesticating and herding animals). The hunting cultures sometimes fished, and usually gathered wild seeds and nuts, but they did not plant or grow vegetables or any other crops. One very rough estimate is 8 million hunters lived circa 9000 BC when the first of several "[agricultural revolutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic_Revolution "Neolithic Revolution")"occurred in the eastern hemisphere (the dates are very conjectural). Around the year 9000 BC in the Middle East,for reasons unknown, some groups began to domesticate and graze sheep. The practice of cultivating plants was invented independently in three places: in the Middle East and Europe (wheat, 6500–3500 BC), in Southeast Asia (rice,6800–4000 BC), and in Central America and Peru (corn, about 2500 BC).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-14)

Agriculture provided a steady food supply that could be stored for a year or longer in order to minimize the risk of famine. Farm production could be expanded by systematic human exertion. The new technology of farming meant that the food supply was proportional to the number of workers who could plant and harvest the crops. Every new pair of hands meant more food for the community, so children were valued in agricultural societies. Later, additional workers found useful work in building irrigation canals and systems that provided a stable water supply for crops, especially in Egypt, Mesopotamia, India, China, Peru and Mexico. The population could now grow because new people paid their own way. (It would take many centuries before the arable land supply became a limiting factor.) However, death rates were high, especially for infants and children, so even with high birth rates growth was slow. The same amount of land could support either 1,000 hunters or 100,000 farmers, and thus farmers ultimately won the fight for the land. Farmers gathered in permanent villages, and through a process of warfare consolidated into much larger states, including those in China, India, Egypt and Mesopotamia. From 300 to 1400 AD large agricultural states also existed throughout the eastern United States, called the "[Hopewell tradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopewell_tradition "Hopewell tradition")" and "[Mississippian cultures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippian_cultures "Mississippian cultures")". They are most famous as [Mound Builders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound_Builders "Mound Builders"), but their culture collapsed (for unknown reasons) by 1500. The natives encountered by the English and French were nomadic hunters who supplemented their meat diet with cultivated vegetables.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-16)

### Ancient and post-classical history

Main articles: [Classical demography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_demography "Classical demography") and [Medieval demography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_demography "Medieval demography")

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Population_curve.svg/500px-Population_curve.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Population_curve.svg)

Graph of human population from 10 000 BC to 2000 [AD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anno_Domini "Anno Domini"). It shows exponential rise in world population that has taken place since the end of the seventeenth century.

Estimates of the population of the world at the time agriculture emerged in around 10,000 BC have ranged between 1 million and 15 million.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-18) Even earlier, genetic evidence suggests humans may have gone through a population bottleneck of between 1,000 and 10,000 people about 70,000 BC, according to the now largely discredited [Toba catastrophe theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toba_catastrophe_theory "Toba catastrophe theory"). By contrast, it is estimated that around 50–60 million people lived in the combined eastern and western [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") in the 4th century AD.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-19)

The [Plague of Justinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plague_of_Justinian "Plague of Justinian") caused Europe's population to drop by around 50% between the 6th and 8th centuries AD.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-20) The population of Europe was more than 70 million in 1340.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-21) From 1340 to 1400, the world's population fell from an estimated 443 million to 350–375 million,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-22) with the [Indian subcontinent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_subcontinent "Indian subcontinent") suffering the most tremendous loss and Europe suffering the [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death")[pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandemic "Pandemic");[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-Essai_sur_l'%C3%A9volution_du_nombre_des_hommes-23) it took 200 years for European population figures to recover.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-24) The population of China decreased from 123 million in 1200 to 65 million in 1393,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-25) presumably from a combination of [Mongol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_Empire "Mongol Empire") invasions, famine, and plague.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-26)

Starting in AD 2, the [Han dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty "Han dynasty") of [ancient China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_China "Ancient China") kept consistent family registers to properly assess the poll taxes and labor service duties of each household.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-nishijima_1986_pp595-96-27) In that year, the population of [Western Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Han "Western Han") was recorded as 57,671,400 individuals in 12,366,470 households, decreasing to 47,566,772 individuals in 9,348,227 households by AD 146, towards the [end of the Han dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_the_Han_dynasty "End of the Han dynasty").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-nishijima_1986_pp595-96-27) From 200 to 400, the world population fell from an estimated 257 million to 206 million, with China suffering the greatest loss.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-Essai_sur_l'%C3%A9volution_du_nombre_des_hommes-23) At the founding of the [Ming dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_dynasty "Ming dynasty") in 1368, China's population was reported to be close to 60 million; toward the end of the dynasty in 1644, it may have approached 150 million.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-28) England's population reached an estimated 5.6 million in 1650, up from an estimated 2.6 million in 1500.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-29) New crops that were brought to Asia and Europe from the Americas by Portuguese and Spanish colonists in the 16th century are believed to have contributed to population growth.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-32) Since their introduction to Africa by Portuguese traders in the 16th century,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-33) maize and [cassava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassava "Cassava") have similarly replaced traditional African crops as the most important [staple food](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staple_food "Staple food") crops grown on the continent.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-34)

The [pre-Columbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Columbian_era "Pre-Columbian era") population of the Americas is uncertain; historian David Henige called it "the most unanswerable question in the world."[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-35) By the end of the 20th century, scholarly consensus favored an estimate of roughly 55 million people, but numbers from various sources have ranged from 10 million to 100 million.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-36) Encounters between European explorers and populations in the rest of the world often introduced local [epidemics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_epidemics "List of epidemics") of extraordinary virulence.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-37) According to the most extreme scholarly claims, as many as 90% of the [Native American population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_history_of_the_Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Population history of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas") of the [New World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World "New World") died of [Old World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_World "Old World") diseases such as [smallpox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox "Smallpox"), [measles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measles "Measles"), and [influenza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Influenza "Influenza").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-38) Over the centuries, the Europeans had developed high degrees of immunity to these diseases, while the indigenous peoples had no such immunity.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-39)

### Modern history

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Cities_with_1M_People_in_2025.png/500px-Cities_with_1M_People_in_2025.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cities_with_1M_People_in_2025.png)

Map showing urban areas with at least one million inhabitants in 2025. Only 3% of the world's population lived in urban areas in 1800; this proportion had risen to 47% by 2000, and reached 56% by 2020.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-40)

During the European [Agricultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Agricultural_Revolution "British Agricultural Revolution") and [Industrial Revolutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution"), the [life expectancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_expectancy "Life expectancy") of children increased dramatically.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-41) The percentage of the children born in London who [died before the age of five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infant_mortality "Infant mortality") decreased from 74.5% in 1730–1749 to 31.8% in 1810–1829.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-Buer-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-43) Between 1700 and 1900, Europe's population increased from about 100 million to over 400 million.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-44) Altogether, the areas populated by people of European descent comprised 36% of the world's population in 1900.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-45)

Population growth in the Western world became more rapid after the introduction of [vaccination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaccination "Vaccination") and other improvements in medicine and [sanitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanitation "Sanitation").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-46) Improved material conditions led to the population of Britain increasing from 10 million to 40 million in the 19th century.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-47) The population of the United Kingdom reached 60 million in 2006.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-48) The United States saw its population grow from around 5.3 million in 1800 to 106 million in 1920, exceeding 307 million in 2010.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-49)

### 20th century

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Global_population_after_1820.png/500px-Global_population_after_1820.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Global_population_after_1820.png)

The human population grew by approximately 4.5 billion people during the 20th century, increasing from about 1.6 billion in 1900 to just over 6 billion by the year 2000.

The first half of the 20th century in [Imperial Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire") and the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") was marked by a succession of major wars, [famines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famine "Famine") and other disasters which caused large-scale population losses (approximately 60 million excess deaths).[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-51) After the collapse of the Soviet Union, Russia's population declined significantly – from 150 million in 1991 to 143 million in 2012[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-52) – but by 2013 this decline appeared to have halted.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-53)

Many countries in the [developing world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developing_world "Developing world") have experienced extremely rapid population growth since the early 20th century, due to economic development and improvements in public health. China's population rose from approximately 430 million in 1850 to 580 million in 1953,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-54) and now stands at over 1.3 billion. The population of the [Indian subcontinent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_subcontinent "Indian subcontinent"), which was about 125 million in 1750, increased to 389 million in 1941;[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-55) today, India, Pakistan and Bangladesh are collectively home to about 1.63 billion people.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-56)[Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java "Java"), an island in [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia"), had about 5 million inhabitants in 1815; it had a population of over 139 million in 2020.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-57) In just one hundred years, the population of Brazil decupled (x10), from about 17 million in 1900, or about 1% of the world population in that year, to about 176 million in 2000, or almost 3% of the global population in the very early 21st century. Mexico's population grew from 13.6 million in 1900 to about 112 million in 2010.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-59) Between the 1920s and 2000s, Kenya's population grew from 2.9 million to 37 million.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-60)

The UN estimated that the world population reached one billion for the first time in 1804. It was another 123 years before it reached two billion in 1927, but it took only 33 years to reach three billion in 1960.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-un2004-62) Thereafter, it took 14 years for the global population to reach four billion in 1974, 13 years to reach five billion in 1987, 12 years to reach six billion in 1999 and, according to the United States Census Bureau, 13 years to reach seven billion in March 2012.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-USCBcite-63) The United Nations, however, estimated that the world population reached seven billion in October 2011.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-UN7bn-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-Guardian7-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-UPI7bn-66)

According to the UN, the global population reached eight billion in November 2022,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-auto-67) but because the growth rate is slowing, it will take another 15 years to reach around 9 billion by 2037 and 20 years to reach 10 billion by 2057.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:7-68) Alternative scenarios for 2050 range from a low of 7.4 billion to a high of more than 10.6 billion.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-WorldPopProspects-69) Projected figures vary depending on underlying statistical assumptions and the variables used in projection calculations, especially the [fertility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fertility "Fertility") and [mortality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortality_rate "Mortality rate") variables. Long-range predictions to 2150 range from a population decline to 3.2 billion in the "low scenario", to "high scenarios" of 24.8 billion.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-WorldPopProspects-69) One extreme scenario predicted a massive increase to 256 billion by 2150, assuming the global fertility rate remained at its 1995 level of 3.04 children per woman; however, by 2010 the global fertility rate had declined to 2.52.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-LongRangeProjections2003KeyFindings-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-Fertility2010-71)

There is no estimation for the exact day or month the world's population surpassed one or two billion. The points at which it reached three and four billion were not officially noted, but the International Database of the United States Census Bureau placed them in July 1959 and April 1974 respectively. The United Nations did determine, and commemorate, the "Day of 5 Billion" on 11 July 1987, and the "Day of 6 Billion" on 12 October 1999. The Population Division of the United Nations declared the "[Day of Seven Billion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_Seven_Billion "Day of Seven Billion")" to be 31 October 2011.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-72) The United Nations marked the birth of the [eight billionth person](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinice_Mabansag "Vinice Mabansag") on 15 November 2022.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-73)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-auto-67)

 2015 map showing average life expectancy by country in years. In 2015, the World Health Organization estimated the average global life expectancy as 71.4 years.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-WHOStats2016-74)

As of 2020, the global [sex ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_sex_ratio "Human sex ratio") is approximately 1.01 males to 1 female.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-cia-factbook-75) Approximately 24.7% of the global population is aged under 15, while 65.2% is aged 15–64 and 10.1% is aged 65 or over.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-cia-factbook-75) The median age of the world's population is estimated to be 31 years in 2020,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-:0-9) and is expected to rise to 37.9 years by 2050.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-76)

According to the [World Health Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Health_Organization "World Health Organization"), the global average [life expectancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_life_expectancy "List of countries by life expectancy") is 73.3 years as of 2020, with women living an average of 75.9 years and men approximately 70.8 years.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-77) In 2010, the global [fertility rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fertility_rate "Fertility rate") was estimated at 2.44 children per woman.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-78) In June 2012, British researchers calculated the total weight of Earth's human population as approximately 287 million tonnes (630 billion pounds), with the average person weighing around 62 kilograms (137 lb).[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-79)

The [IMF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund "International Monetary Fund") estimated nominal 2021 [gross world product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_world_product "Gross world product") at US$94.94 trillion, giving an annual global per capita figure of around US$12,290.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-80) Around 9.3% of the world population lives in [extreme poverty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_poverty "Extreme poverty"), subsisting on less than US$1.9 per day;[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-81) around 8.9% are [malnourished](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malnutrition "Malnutrition").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-82) 87% of the world's over-15s are considered [literate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literacy_rate "Literacy rate").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-83) As of January 2024, there were about 5 billion global Internet users, constituting 66% of the world population.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-84)

The [Han Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Chinese "Han Chinese") are the world's largest single ethnic group, constituting over 19% of the global population in 2011.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-85) The world's most-spoken languages[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-86) are [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language") (1.132B), [Mandarin Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandarin_Chinese "Mandarin Chinese") (1.117B), [Hindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi "Hindi") (615M), [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language") (534M) and [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language") (280M). More than three billion people speak an Indo-European language, which is the largest language family by number of speakers. Standard Arabic is a language with no native speakers, but the total number of speakers is estimated at 274 million people.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-87)

The largest religious categories in the world as of 2020 are estimated as follows: [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") (31%), [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") (25%), [Unaffiliated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irreligion "Irreligion") (16%) and [Hinduism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinduism "Hinduism") (15%).[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-Pew-88)

Population by continent (2022 data)

Six of the Earth's seven [continents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continent "Continent") are permanently inhabited on a large scale. Asia is the most populous continent, with its 4.64 billion inhabitants accounting for 60% of the world population. The world's two most populated countries, India and China, together constitute about 36% of the world's population. Africa is the second most populated continent, with around 1.34 billion people, or 17% of the world's population. Europe's 747 million people make up 10% of the world's population as of 2020, while the [Latin American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_American "Latin American") and [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean") regions are home to around 653 million (8%). Northern America, primarily consisting of the United States and Canada, has a population of around 368 million (5%), and Oceania, the least populated region, has about 42 million inhabitants (0.5%).[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-89)[Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica "Antarctica") only has a very small, fluctuating population of about 1200 people based mainly in polar [science stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_stations_in_Antarctica "Research stations in Antarctica").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population#cite_note-AntarcticCIA-90)
